title: The Mastery Roadmap
subtitle: PREVIEW — a map of everything ahead: 10 phases, the 17-question lesson blueprint, 4 interfaces
mantra: Learn Databricks in dependency order — compute up to CI/CD — and attack every feature with the same 17 questions.
objectives: You can list the 10 phases in dependency order and explain why compute comes first.
You can recite the 17-question lesson blueprint and use it to learn any new feature.
You can sort any command or setting into SQL, PySpark, platform config or CLI.
You can give a crisp 1–2 line definition of every term the roadmap mentions (Auto Loader, AQE, ABAC, Bundles…).
You can walk the PERMISSION_DENIED, task-failed and slow-job debugging chains in order.
You can answer both certification-style and engineering-style (skew) questions.

sections.title: Phase 1 — Compute Mastery (Preview)

blocks.text: **Goal:** understand compute deeply enough to configure, reason about, troubleshoot and optimize real Spark workloads — understand **every field**, not just the names.

blocks.title: Official compute split
blocks.text: Databricks officially splits compute into **serverless**, **classic** and **SQL warehouses**. Classic compute includes **all-purpose**, **jobs** and **Lakeflow pipeline** resources.

The JVM process on a worker that runs tasks and holds cached/shuffle data.

One executor core = one slot = one task running concurrently.
A chunk of data; one task processes one partition.
The VM instance type (cores, RAM, disk) chosen for workers / for the driver.
Databricks adds/removes workers between a min and max based on load.
Pre-warmed idle instances that make clusters start and scale faster.
Spot: cheap spare capacity that can be reclaimed. On-demand: full price, not reclaimed.

Isolation/sharing model — **Standard** (multi-user, shared) or **Dedicated** (single user or group).
Stopping the cluster; auto-termination stops it after N idle minutes to save cost.
VM types, worker counts, spot/on-demand, runtime image and cluster startup — Databricks manages them.
Mainly your code, the **environment** (environment version + Python dependencies) and a few job/notebook settings.

blocks.label: Think first: with workers min 2 / max 10, 8 cores each, how many tasks can run at once?
blocks.text: Only **worker** cores run tasks: 2 × 8 = **16** slots at minimum, 10 × 8 = **80** at maximum. The driver's 16 cores schedule work; they do not add task slots.

blocks.title: Don't count the driver
blocks.text: A classic mistake in parallelism math is adding driver cores to the task slots. Tasks run on **executors on workers**.
**Immediate next lesson — Compute Part 3: From VM to Spark Task.** Config: driver + 4 workers, 8 cores and 32 GB RAM per worker, DBR 18 LTS, Photon enabled, autoscale 2–8.

Where is the executor heap? What is memory overhead?

blocks.title: Too few partitions
blocks.text: With fewer partitions than task slots, cores sit idle no matter how big the cluster is.

blocks.label: Think first: 4 workers × 8 cores, a stage with 1,000 partitions vs 4 partitions?
blocks.text: 32 slots. 1,000 partitions → tasks run in about ⌈1000/32⌉ = **32 waves**. 4 partitions → only **4 tasks**, so 28 cores sit **idle** — too few partitions waste the cluster.

blocks.title: insertInto is positional
blocks.text: `insertInto` maps columns **by position**, not by name. If the DataFrame's column order differs from the table's, values silently land in the wrong columns (or fail on type).

items.def: Append adds rows; overwrite replaces the table's (or a partition's) contents.
Overwrite only the partitions present in the incoming data (`partitionOverwriteMode=dynamic`), leaving others untouched.
A MERGE you can re-run on the same input without creating duplicates or double-applying changes.
Change Data Capture: a feed of inserts/updates/deletes to apply to a target.
Keep one row per key (e.g. `ROW_NUMBER()` over key ordered by timestamp).
Records that arrive after newer records for the same key/time — must not overwrite newer state.
Delta rejects writes whose schema doesn't match the table.
Explicitly allow new columns to be added on write (e.g. `mergeSchema`).
Change a column to a wider type (e.g. INT → BIGINT) without rewriting data files.
Query an older snapshot: `VERSION AS OF` / `TIMESTAMP AS OF`.
Mark rows as deleted/changed in a side file instead of rewriting the whole Parquet file immediately.
Too many tiny files → metadata, file-open and task-scheduling overhead.
Compacts small files into larger ones (and applies clustering).
Uses per-file statistics to skip files that cannot contain matching rows.
Min/max/null counts per column stored in the Delta log for each file.
Flexible, incremental data layout by clustering keys (`CLUSTER BY`) — keys can change without a full rewrite; replaces static partitioning/Z-order.
For Unity Catalog managed tables, Databricks automatically runs OPTIMIZE / VACUUM / ANALYZE when it judges they're needed.

blocks.title: OPTIMIZE ≠ VACUUM
blocks.text: **OPTIMIZE** reorganizes active files/layout. **VACUUM** physically deletes expired, unreferenced files. History is not a backup — VACUUM and retention remove old files.

Incremental file ingestion as a stream: processes only new files that land in a directory.

blocks.title: "Exactly-once-ish"
blocks.text: Exactly-once ingestion depends on the **checkpoint**. Delete or change it and Auto Loader treats every file as new → **duplicates**.

Was the checkpoint deleted, moved or shared between two streams?
Did the source schema change (new/renamed columns)?
Is anything sitting in `_rescued_data`?

blocks.title: Why exactly-once is subtle
blocks.text: End-to-end exactly-once needs a **replayable source + checkpoint + idempotent/transactional sink**. You can still create duplicates: deleting/changing the checkpoint, two queries writing the same table, non-idempotent `foreachBatch` logic, or duplicates already in the source.

blocks.label: Think first: you restart a stream with a NEW checkpoint path on the same source. What happens?
blocks.text: The new query has no memory of processed offsets/files, so it starts from the beginning (or from the configured starting point) and **reprocesses data → duplicates** in an append sink.

blocks.text: **Goal:** master SQL analytics and BI compute rather than treating SQL warehouses as a black box.

Saved SQL statements you can reuse, schedule and share.
List of past queries with status, duration, user and warehouse.
Visual per-operator breakdown of a query's execution — the DBSQL debugging tool.
Compute for SQL: **Serverless**, **Pro** or **Classic**.
T-shirt size (2X-Small … 4X-Large) of each cluster → speed of individual queries.
How many clusters the warehouse scales across → concurrency (many users).
Adds clusters under load / stops the warehouse after idle minutes.
Databricks' native dashboards built on SQL datasets.
Scheduled query + condition that sends a notification when met.

points: Compute runs in your cloud account

blocks.title: Wrong warehouse knob
blocks.text: Raising **size** doesn't fix queueing, and raising **max clusters** doesn't fix one heavy query.

blocks.title: Size vs clusters
blocks.text: **Size** makes each query faster (bigger cluster). **Max clusters** lets more queries run at once (concurrency). Queries *queueing* → raise max clusters; one *heavy* query slow → bigger size or tune the query.

blocks.title: SQL performance tuning
blocks.text: Phase 8 ends with SQL performance tuning — start from the **query profile**, not by guessing.

sections.title: Phase 9 — Performance & Debugging (Preview)
sections.hook: "Job went from 8 to 42 minutes" — evidence, not a bigger cluster.

blocks.text: One of the most important units for **interviews and real work**. Driven by real **symptom** cases.

blocks.code:
Job used to take 8 min.
Now takes 42 min.
blocks.caption: Example case

blocks.title: Not: "use a bigger cluster"
blocks.text: **Goal:** diagnose slowdowns using **evidence** instead of blindly scaling compute.

Query slow
   ↓
Spark UI
   ↓
Find slow stage
   ↓
Find slow tasks
   ↓
Compare task distribution
   ↓
Skew? Shuffle? Spill? I/O?
Join? GC? Small files?
blocks.caption: Investigation process

head: Spark UI metric
What it tells you
rows: Hierarchy: action → stages split at shuffles → one task per partition.
Bytes read from the source by the stage/task.
Bytes written by map-side tasks for the next stage.
Bytes fetched by reduce-side tasks — uneven = skew.
Size (in memory, deserialized) of data that had to be spilled.
Size of that spilled data on disk (serialized) — any spill = memory pressure.
Time the JVM paused for garbage collection — high → memory pressure.
Compare min/median/max — a long tail = skew or stragglers.
Rows read/written per task — reveals uneven partitions.

head: Plan operator
Meaning
rows: A shuffle (or broadcast) — data redistributed; stage boundary.
Small side copied to every executor; big side not shuffled.
Both sides shuffled by key, sorted, then merged — the large-large join.
Aggregation with a hash map (often partial → Exchange → final).
Reading the source; shows pushed filters / files read.
Row predicate applied to the data.
`WholeStageCodegen` / `*(n)`: fuses several operators into one generated function.
`Photon...` nodes run in the Photon engine; non-Photon nodes show fallbacks.

items.def: A few keys/partitions hold far more data than others → a few very slow tasks.
Append a random suffix to a hot key to spread it across many partitions.
Send a small table to all executors to avoid shuffling the big one.
Adaptive Query Execution: re-optimizes at runtime — coalesces shuffle partitions, switches join strategy, splits skewed partitions.
Choose a sensible number/size of partitions (e.g. `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions`).
repartition = full shuffle to N partitions (up or down); coalesce = merge partitions without full shuffle (down only).
Many tiny files slow reads; compaction (`OPTIMIZE`) merges them.
Skip irrelevant files via stats; cluster data so skipping works well.
Driver runs out of memory — e.g. `collect()`/`toPandas()` of big data, huge broadcast, too much metadata.
An executor runs out of memory — e.g. a giant skewed partition, oversized partitions.
Memory too tight: lots of GC time, data spilled to disk.

head: Bound by
Typical evidence
rows: Cores busy, little spill/IO wait; heavy UDFs, decompression, complex expressions.
Time dominated by reading/writing storage or shuffle fetch; many small files.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when a job got slower
questions: What changed: data volume, code, cluster, runtime?
Which stage got slow?
Inside that stage, are ALL tasks slow or only a few?
Is shuffle read/write much bigger than before?
Is there spill or high GC time?
Is the join strategy what I expected (broadcast vs sort-merge)?
Did the number/size of input files explode (small files)?

sections.title: Phase 10 — Production Engineering, CLI & CI/CD (Preview)
sections.hook: Not a developer who only knows how to press ‘Run All’.

blocks.text: **Goal:** move beyond notebooks and operate Databricks as a **production software platform**.

items.def: Command-line tool (`databricks ...`) to manage workspace objects, jobs, bundles, etc.
Clone a Git repo into the workspace and commit/pull/branch from there (formerly *Repos*).
Non-notebook files (`.py`, `.yml`, `.json`) stored in the workspace.
Reusable `.py` code imported by notebooks/jobs instead of copy-paste.
Packaged library (`.whl`) installed on compute.
Pinning libraries per cluster/job/serverless environment for reproducible runs.
Run Spark code from your local IDE against remote Databricks compute.
Develop locally (e.g. VS Code), test, then deploy.

blocks.title: Declarative Automation Bundles
blocks.text: Per the source, the **current name of the former Databricks Asset Bundles (DABs)**. You describe jobs, pipelines, source files, deployment targets and other resources as **version-controlled configuration**, then validate and deploy via CI/CD.

blocks.code:
bundle:
  name: orders_project

resources:
  jobs:
    orders_job:          # resource KEY
      name: orders-job   # display name
      tasks:
        ...

targets:
  dev:
    mode: development
  prod:
    mode: production
blocks.caption: databricks.yml — the primary bundle file (YAML)

blocks.code:
databricks bundle validate
databricks bundle deploy -t dev
databricks bundle run orders_job -t dev
blocks.caption: Bundle commands

head: Command
Does
rows: Checks the bundle configuration for errors before deploying.
Uploads files and creates/updates resources in the `dev` target.
Runs the deployed resource identified by its **key** in the `dev` target.

blocks.title: Key, not display name
blocks.text: `bundle run` takes the resource **key** (`orders_job`), not the job's display `name` (`orders-job`).

blocks.title: Target modes
blocks.text: `mode: development` deploys per-user copies (names prefixed with `[dev user]`, schedules paused). `mode: production` is for the real deployment, ideally run as a **service principal**.

blocks.title: Personal identity in CI/CD
blocks.text: Deploying or running production with a person's token is risky and breaks when people leave or change roles. Use a **service principal** as the deployment identity.

items.def: Feature branches → PR → main; deployments come from tracked commits.
Run `bundle validate` + unit/integration tests in CI before deploy.
Per-target settings (catalog, cluster size, schedule) in the bundle.
Separate environments; promote the same code through them.
Prod deploys and runs under a non-human identity, not a person's account.
Same commit → same deployment; roll back by redeploying a previous version.
Credentials kept in secret scopes, never hard-coded.
Branch → CI validate/test → deploy to test → approve → deploy to prod.

sections.title: Assessment Strategy: Certification vs Engineering Questions
sections.hook: Two kinds of questions — the second kind is what makes you genuinely good.

items.title: Certification-style
points: e.g. which compute for a scheduled job?

items.title: Engineering-style
points: Form a hypothesis, prove it with evidence

blocks.text: **Certification example:** *You need to run a scheduled PySpark workload without managing infrastructure. Which compute should you use?* → **Serverless Jobs** (serverless job compute).
**Engineering example:** *A 2 TB ETL job went from 12 to 45 minutes. One stage has 1,000 tasks; 997 finish in 20 seconds, 3 run for 15 minutes while spilling 80 GB each.*

blocks.title: Expected reasoning
blocks.text: **Likely data skew.** Then know *why*, *how to prove it in the Spark UI* and *which fixes exist*.

blocks.title: How to answer
blocks.text: Name the hypothesis (skew), show the evidence (median ≈ 20 s vs max ≈ 15 min, shuffle read and spill concentrated in 3 tasks), find the hot key (e.g. one huge customer or NULLs), then fixes: AQE skew-join handling, salting, broadcasting the small side, handling hot keys/NULLs separately.

blocks.title: Ask yourself on a straggler stage
questions: Are only a few tasks slow while most are fast?
Do those tasks read far more shuffle data/records?
Are they the ones spilling?
Which join or groupBy key feeds that stage?
Is one key value (or NULL) dominating?
Does the plan show a SortMergeJoin that could be broadcast?

blocks.title: More hardware ≠ fix for skew
blocks.text: Adding workers doesn't help: the 3 huge partitions are still processed by 3 single tasks.

debug.title: How to learn ANY new Databricks feature (the 17 questions)
debug.symptom: You meet a new feature (Auto Loader, AUTO CDC, Bundles…) and the information feels scattered: you know names and slides but couldn't build or debug it.
askYourself: What problem are we solving?
How would I solve it without Databricks?
Which Databricks component solves it?
How does it work internally?
Where does it sit in the architecture?
How do I use it in the UI?
What is the real syntax?
What does a production example look like?
What alternatives exist?
When should I NOT use it?
What are the best practices?
What are the common mistakes?
What is the debugging workflow?
What are the certification traps?
Have I done the exercises?
Have I checked the full solutions?
How do I extend the mini-project with it?

steps.do: WHY (1–3): write one sentence for the problem and sketch the manual, non-Databricks solution.
steps.why: Anchors the feature to a real need and shows what it automates.

steps.do: HOW (4–5): draw where it runs (control plane, compute, storage, catalog) and its internal state.
steps.why: Internals explain behavior and failure modes.

steps.do: USE (6–8): find it in the UI, write the real syntax, read a production example.
steps.why: The tutor insists most on 6–8: no lesson without a real config or source file.

steps.do: JUDGE (9–12): list alternatives, when NOT to use, best practices, common mistakes.
steps.why: Knowing the boundary of a tool is what interviews test.

steps.do: BREAK (13–14): break it on purpose, write the ordered debug checklist, note exam traps.
steps.why: Debugging is top priority for real work.

steps.do: PROVE (15–17): do exercises, compare with full solutions, add it to the e-commerce lakehouse.
steps.why: The growing project ties every feature into one system.

rootCauses: Skipping ‘when NOT to use’ and debugging
debug.fix: Walk the 17 questions in order, with special weight on 6–8 (UI, syntax, production example) and 13 (debugging).
debug.mnemonic: WHY → HOW → USE → JUDGE → BREAK → PROVE

debug.title: PERMISSION_DENIED on a Unity Catalog object
debug.symptom: A query or job fails with `PERMISSION_DENIED` (e.g. reading `prod.silver.orders`), often while the same code works for you interactively.
askYourself: Who am I right now?
Which principal is the job/pipeline actually running as?
Does that principal have USE CATALOG on the catalog?
Does it have USE SCHEMA on the schema?
Does it have SELECT (read) or MODIFY (write) on the object?
Does the operation need ownership (ALTER, DROP, grant)?
For path-based/external data: is the storage credential / external location granted?

steps.do: Check your own identity.
steps.why: Confirms who you are testing as.

steps.do: Check the job's run-as identity in the job settings.
steps.why: Jobs may run as the owner or a service principal, not you.

steps.do: Show grants top-down: catalog → schema → table.
steps.why: SELECT alone is useless without USE CATALOG + USE SCHEMA.

steps.do: Check ownership if the operation is ALTER/DROP.
steps.why: Some operations require being the owner.

steps.do: For external paths check the external location and storage credential grants.
steps.why: Data access to cloud paths goes through them.

steps.do: Grant the minimal missing privilege.
steps.why: Least privilege.
steps.code: GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA prod.silver TO `sp-etl`;

rootCauses: Job runs as a different principal
Missing USE CATALOG or USE SCHEMA
Missing grant on external location/storage credential
debug.fix: Identify the real principal, walk USE CATALOG → USE SCHEMA → SELECT/MODIFY → ownership → storage credential, and grant only the missing privilege (preferably to a group or service principal).
debug.mnemonic: WHO → WHICH → CATALOG → SCHEMA → OBJECT → OWNER → STORAGE

debug.title: A Lakeflow Job task failed
debug.symptom: A job run is red: one task failed (e.g. `gold`), downstream tasks were skipped.
askYourself: Did an upstream task fail or produce bad output?
Did the compute start correctly?
Is it a runtime (DBR) issue?
Is a library missing or conflicting?
Does the run-as identity have the permissions?
Was a parameter missing or wrong?
Is the input data unexpected?
Is it a Spark execution problem (OOM, skew, timeout)?

steps.do: Open the failed run and the task's error output.
steps.why: The error class usually points to one bucket.

steps.do: Check upstream task runs and their outputs.
steps.why: Many failures are just propagated bad inputs.

steps.do: Check cluster events / compute start, runtime version and libraries.
steps.why: Infra and dependency issues are cheap to rule out.

steps.do: Check the run-as principal and grants.
steps.why: Jobs often run as a different identity.

steps.do: Check resolved parameters and input data.
steps.why: Wrong date parameter or schema drift breaks code.

steps.do: Only then open the Spark UI for execution issues.
steps.why: Deepest, most expensive check last.

debug.fix: Walk the model in order; fix the specific bucket (e.g. declare the library in the job environment, grant the principal, correct the parameter) and repair-run the failed tasks.

debug.title: Job got slow: 8 min → 42 min
debug.symptom: A job that used to take 8 minutes now takes 42; nothing obviously failed.
askYourself: What changed: data volume, code, cluster, runtime?
Which stage became slow?
Are all tasks in that stage slow, or only a few?
Did shuffle read/write grow?
Is there spill (memory/disk) or high GC time?
Did the join strategy change (BroadcastHashJoin → SortMergeJoin)?
Is it I/O: many small files or a huge scan?

steps.do: Open the Spark UI and sort stages by duration.
steps.why: Find where the time went.

steps.do: Inside the slow stage, read summary metrics (min/median/max).
steps.why: Uniform vs long-tail distribution separates volume/plan issues from skew.

steps.do: Check shuffle read/write, spill and GC time.
steps.why: Reveals shuffle growth and memory pressure.

steps.do: Read the physical plan (Exchange, join type, Scan).
steps.why: Plan changes explain sudden slowdowns.

steps.do: Check input file counts/sizes.
steps.why: Small files make jobs I/O-bound.

steps.do: Apply the targeted fix (AQE, broadcast, salting, compaction, partition tuning).
steps.why: Evidence-driven instead of blind scaling.

rootCauses: Too few or too many partitions
debug.fix: Locate stage → tasks → distribution, confirm the hypothesis with metrics and the plan, and fix the cause rather than adding hardware.
debug.mnemonic: Stage → Tasks → Spread → (Skew Shuffle Spill IO Join GC Files)

debug.title: Spark UI checklist: a few straggler tasks (skew)
debug.symptom: 1,000 tasks: 997 finish in ~20 s, 3 run for 15 minutes and spill 80 GB each; the job went from 12 to 45 minutes.
askYourself: Are only a few tasks slow while most are fast?
Do the slow tasks read far more shuffle data and records?
Are the slow tasks the ones spilling?
Is GC time high only on those tasks?
Which join or grouping key feeds this stage?
Does one key value (or NULL) dominate?
Does the physical plan show a SortMergeJoin that could be a broadcast?

steps.do: Stage page → Summary metrics: compare median vs max duration.
steps.why: Max ≫ median = long tail.

steps.do: Compare shuffle read size / records per task.
steps.why: Uneven shuffle read proves uneven partitions.

steps.do: Check spill (memory/disk) and GC time per task.
steps.why: Huge partitions don't fit in execution memory.

steps.do: Count rows per key on the join/group key.
steps.why: Finds the hot key.

steps.do: Read the physical plan for the join strategy.
steps.why: Broadcasting the small side removes the shuffle of the big side.

steps.do: Fix: AQE skew join, salting, broadcast, or separate hot-key/NULL handling.
steps.why: Redistributes the work.

rootCauses: Shuffle join where broadcast is possible
debug.fix: Prove skew from task-duration distribution, shuffle read and spill, find the hot key, then use AQE skew handling, salting or broadcasting — not more workers.

debug.title: Ingestion broke: missing, duplicate, drifted or malformed data
debug.symptom: Bronze has missing rows, every row twice, new columns not appearing, or garbage values after an Auto Loader / COPY INTO load.
askYourself: Which symptom is it: missing, duplicate, schema drift or malformed rows?
Did the files really land in the path the stream reads?
Was the checkpoint deleted, moved, or shared between two streams?
Did the source schema change (new/renamed/retyped columns)?
Is anything sitting in `_rescued_data`?
Am I using an explicit schema or inference/hints?

steps.do: Classify the symptom and find affected files/rows.
steps.why: Each symptom has a different root cause.

steps.do: List the source path and compare with what was ingested.
steps.why: Missing data is often files in the wrong place.

steps.do: Verify checkpointLocation is unchanged and unique per stream.
steps.why: A new/shared checkpoint causes re-ingestion → duplicates.

steps.do: Inspect the schema in schemaLocation and the stream's schema-evolution behavior.
steps.why: New columns stop the stream until restart (default mode).

steps.do: Query rows where `_rescued_data IS NOT NULL`.
steps.why: Shows values that didn't fit the schema.

debug.fix: Keep one stable checkpoint per stream, use schemaLocation + hints (or explicit schema), monitor `_rescued_data`, and repair data with dedup or RESTORE.

debug.title: Duplicates in a streaming target after restart
debug.symptom: After a restart or failure, a streaming Delta table contains duplicate events.
askYourself: Did the checkpoint location change or get deleted?
Is another query writing to the same target?
Is my foreachBatch logic idempotent?
Did the source itself deliver duplicates?
Do I need dedup with a watermark?

steps.do: Compare the checkpointLocation before and after the restart.
steps.why: A new checkpoint restarts from the beginning.

steps.do: Check DESCRIBE HISTORY on the target for unexpected writers.
steps.why: Two queries with different checkpoints double-write.

steps.do: Review foreachBatch code for plain INSERTs.
steps.why: Retried batches re-run non-idempotent writes; use MERGE on a key.

steps.do: Check the source for duplicates and add dedup (with watermark) if needed.
steps.why: Exactly-once can't remove duplicates already in the source.

debug.fix: Keep one stable checkpoint per query, make custom writes idempotent (MERGE), dedup with a watermark when the source can duplicate, and clean up with dedup/RESTORE.

pitfalls.title: Following the menu instead of dependencies
pitfalls.text: Learning in workspace-menu order presents concepts before their prerequisites.
pitfalls.fix: Follow dependency order: Compute → Delta → UC → Ingestion → Streaming → Pipelines → Jobs → SQL → Performance → CI/CD.

pitfalls.title: Names without syntax
pitfalls.text: Two lessons on a tool without seeing a real config or source file leave you unable to use it.
pitfalls.fix: Always cover lesson questions 6–8: UI, real syntax, production example.

pitfalls.title: Counting driver cores as task slots
pitfalls.text: Only executor cores on workers run tasks; adding the driver's cores overestimates parallelism.
pitfalls.fix: Task slots ≈ workers × cores per worker.

pitfalls.title: Too few partitions
pitfalls.text: 4 partitions on 32 cores leave 28 cores idle.
pitfalls.fix: Have at least as many (similar-size) partitions as task slots; usually several times more.

pitfalls.title: insertInto is positional
pitfalls.text: `insertInto` maps columns by position; a different column order silently corrupts data.
pitfalls.fix: Select columns in table order or use `saveAsTable`/`writeTo`, which resolve by name.

pitfalls.title: OPTIMIZE vs VACUUM confusion
pitfalls.text: OPTIMIZE re-lays out active files; VACUUM deletes unreferenced files physically.
pitfalls.fix: Compaction → OPTIMIZE; storage cleanup → VACUUM (mind the retention).

pitfalls.title: SELECT alone is not enough
pitfalls.text: Without USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA the table is unreachable even with SELECT.
pitfalls.fix: Grant USE CATALOG + USE SCHEMA + SELECT (or inherit from above).

pitfalls.title: ‘It works for me’ ≠ the job has access
pitfalls.text: Jobs can run as the owner or a service principal with different grants.
pitfalls.fix: Always check the job's run-as principal first.

pitfalls.title: Changing/deleting a checkpoint
pitfalls.text: Auto Loader and streams lose their memory of processed data → full re-ingestion and duplicates.
pitfalls.fix: Treat checkpoint paths as fixed, one per stream.

pitfalls.title: Batch Auto Loader read
pitfalls.text: `spark.read.format("cloudFiles")` is wrong: Auto Loader is a streaming source.

pitfalls.title: Believing exactly-once means no duplicates
pitfalls.text: Duplicates still arise from new checkpoints, multiple writers, non-idempotent foreachBatch or a duplicating source.
pitfalls.fix: Stable checkpoints, idempotent writes (MERGE), dedup with watermark.

pitfalls.title: Streaming table without STREAM
pitfalls.text: `FROM read_files(...)` without STREAM is a batch query and can't define a streaming table.

pitfalls.title: Legacy names confusion
pitfalls.text: DLT, Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines and Spark Declarative Pipelines are the same product line; APPLY CHANGES is now AUTO CDC.
pitfalls.fix: Learn the current names, recognize the old ones in tutorials.

pitfalls.title: Production jobs on all-purpose compute
pitfalls.text: Interactive clusters are pricier and less isolated, and hide missing job dependencies.
pitfalls.fix: Use serverless job compute or job clusters; declare libraries in the job.

pitfalls.title: Wrong warehouse knob
pitfalls.text: Bigger size doesn't fix queueing; more clusters doesn't fix one heavy query.
pitfalls.fix: Queueing → max clusters; one slow query → query profile, size, layout.

pitfalls.title: Scaling blindly
pitfalls.text: Adding workers doesn't fix skew: a huge partition is still one task.
pitfalls.fix: Spark UI → slow stage → task distribution → targeted fix (AQE, salting, broadcast).

pitfalls.title: bundle run with the display name
pitfalls.text: `databricks bundle run orders-job` uses the job's name instead of its resource key.

pitfalls.title: Deploying prod with a personal identity
pitfalls.text: Personal credentials in CI/CD are risky and break when people leave.
pitfalls.fix: Deploy and run production as a service principal.

exercises.explain: Sources are raw feeds (customers CDC, orders JSON, products CSV, events stream). Bronze keeps raw copies (`*_raw`), silver holds cleaned entities, gold holds business aggregates like `daily_revenue` and `customer_360`.

exercises.q: Compute Part 3 config: 4 workers × 8 cores each (plus a driver). Roughly how many Spark tasks can run concurrently?
exercises.explain: Task slots = worker cores = 4 × 8 = 32 (one task per executor core). The driver schedules tasks but does not run them, so its cores are not counted.

exercises.q: Phase 1 practice config: driver 16 cores; workers 8 cores each, min 2, max 10. What is the MAXIMUM number of concurrent task slots?
exercises.explain: Only worker cores count: 10 × 8 = 80. Adding the driver's 16 (= 96) is the classic trap. At minimum scale you'd have 2 × 8 = 16 slots.

exercises.q: With 32 task slots, a stage has 1,000 partitions of similar size. About how many ‘waves’ of tasks are needed?
exercises.explain: Each wave runs up to 32 tasks: 1000 / 32 = 31.25, so 32 waves (the last one partial). Many partitions keep all cores busy; too few would leave cores idle.

exercises.q: With a 16-core driver and 2 workers of 8 cores, the cluster can run 32 tasks in parallel.
exercises.explain: False. Tasks run on executors on the workers: 2 × 8 = 16 slots. The driver's cores coordinate (planning, scheduling, collecting results) and don't add task slots.

exercises.q: 4 workers × 8 cores, but the stage has only 4 partitions. What happens?
exercises.explain: One task per partition → only 4 tasks, so 28 of 32 cores sit idle. Too few partitions waste the cluster no matter how big it is — that's why partition count is part of compute mastery.

exercises.q: Which output mode writes the ENTIRE result table on every trigger?

exercises.explain: False — that's why the plan says exactly-once is subtle. Exactly-once holds for a given query + checkpoint + transactional sink. exercises.q: After a restart, the streaming table `bronze.events` contains a block of duplicated events.

exercises.q: Streaming table or materialized view?
exercises.explain: Streaming tables process append-only/streaming input once per row — ideal for bronze ingestion with `STREAM read_files`. Materialized views keep the result of any query (joins, aggregations) correct on refresh — ideal for gold aggregates.

items.text: Join of customers and orders kept correct

exercises.q: This pipeline definition fails. Which line is wrong?
exercises.explain: A streaming table must be defined by a streaming query. `read_files(...)` without `STREAM` is a batch read; it should be `FROM STREAM read_files(...)`.
lines: CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE bronze_orders

exercises.q: Write the SQL pipeline definition of a streaming table `bronze_orders` that incrementally reads files with `read_files(...)`.
exercises.explain: `CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE … AS SELECT * FROM STREAM read_files(...)` is the canonical bronze ingestion pattern; STREAM makes it incremental (Auto Loader under the hood).
exercises.solution:
CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE bronze_orders
AS
SELECT *
FROM STREAM read_files(...);

exercises.q: Match the pipeline concept to its definition.
exercises.explain: Expectations are data-quality rules; AUTO CDC applies change feeds; SCD1 overwrites; SCD2 keeps history; the event log records progress/quality/lineage; temporary views are intermediate and not published.
pairs: Data-quality rules: warn, DROP ROW or FAIL UPDATE
Declarative apply of a change feed (formerly APPLY CHANGES)
Overwrite old values, keep current state only
Queryable record of progress, quality metrics, errors
Intermediate dataset not published to the catalog

exercises.q: Delta Live Tables and Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines are two unrelated products.
exercises.explain: False. They are the same product line renamed: Delta Live Tables → Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines → Spark Declarative Pipelines. Old tutorials (DLT, `import dlt`, APPLY CHANGES) still describe the same concepts.

exercises.q: A customer moves from Athens to Thessaloniki. You must keep BOTH addresses with validity periods for historical reports. Which pattern?
exercises.explain: SCD Type 2 keeps history by closing the old row and inserting a new version. SCD Type 1 would overwrite Athens with Thessaloniki and lose history. AUTO CDC supports both via its SCD type setting.

exercises.q: Which is NOT a dataset type you define in a declarative pipeline?
exercises.explain: Streaming tables, materialized views and temporary views are pipeline datasets. A SQL warehouse is compute for Databricks SQL, not a dataset.

exercises.q: Complete the expectation that drops rows with a NULL order_id.
exercises.explain: Expectations are declared as `CONSTRAINT name EXPECT (condition)`; `ON VIOLATION DROP ROW` drops bad rows (default is to keep and only record them; `FAIL UPDATE` stops the update). Violations are counted in the event log.
exercises.text:
CONSTRAINT valid_id [[EXPECT]] (order_id IS NOT NULL)
  ON [[VIOLATION]] [[DROP ROW]]

exercises.q: Match the job trigger to when it starts a run.
exercises.explain: Schedules are time-based; continuous keeps one run always going; file-arrival reacts to new files in storage; table-update reacts to changes in monitored tables.
pairs: Immediately after the previous run ends
When new files land in a monitored location
When a monitored source table changes

exercises.q: Order the tasks of the example job DAG (customers and orders run in parallel — treat them as one step).
exercises.explain: ingest → bronze → (customers ‖ orders) → gold → quality check. gold depends on both silver tasks; the quality check runs last on the final outputs.

exercises.q: Order the ‘task failed’ debugging model.
exercises.explain: Upstream first (cheapest), then infrastructure (compute, runtime, library), then identity (permissions), then inputs (parameters, data), and finally Spark execution itself.

exercises.q: Nightly job `orders_daily`: task `gold` fails with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'holidays'`.

steps.prompt: Which bucket of the debugging model is this?

options.text: Library
options.fb: A missing Python module is a dependency/library problem.

options.text: Permissions
options.fb: A permission error would say PERMISSION_DENIED / access denied.

options.text: Data
options.fb: Data issues show up as schema/value errors, not missing modules.

steps.prompt: The task runs fine on your all-purpose cluster. Why does the job fail?

options.text: The job's compute (job cluster / serverless environment) doesn't have the library installed
options.fb: Each compute has its own libraries; your interactive cluster's packages don't follow the job.

options.text: The job runs an older Spark that can't import Python
options.fb: All runtimes run Python; it's the missing package.

options.text: Retries are disabled
options.fb: Retrying won't install the library.

steps.prompt: Best production fix?

options.text: Declare the dependency in the job's task libraries / serverless environment (ideally pinned, in the bundle)
options.fb: Reproducible: the dependency is part of the job definition.

options.text: Point the job at your all-purpose cluster
options.fb: Works by accident, costs more and isn't isolated or reproducible.

options.text: `pip install` inside the notebook manually once
options.fb: Manual one-off steps aren't reproducible.

exercises.q: Where does each job compute option sit?
exercises.explain: Serverless job compute is Databricks-managed. New job clusters, shared job clusters and existing all-purpose clusters are classic compute you configure; only the job clusters are created for the run and terminated after.

exercises.q: Match the Jobs concept to its definition.
exercises.explain: A job is the definition, a task a unit of work, a run one execution; dynamic value references are resolved at run time; run-job triggers another job; for-each loops a nested task.
pairs: One unit of work inside a job
Placeholder like {{job.run_id}} resolved at run time
A task that triggers another job
Runs a nested task once per list item

exercises.q: Running production jobs on an existing all-purpose cluster is the recommended default.
exercises.explain: False. All-purpose compute is meant for interactive work: it's pricier and shared/less isolated. Production jobs normally use serverless job compute or job clusters created per run.

exercises.q: Match the Databricks SQL feature to its purpose.
exercises.explain: Query history lists past runs; the query profile breaks one query down by operator; alerts notify on conditions; AI/BI dashboards visualize; the Statement Execution API runs SQL over REST; JDBC/ODBC connect BI tools.
pairs: List of past queries with duration and user
Per-operator execution breakdown of one query
Notify when a scheduled query meets a condition
Run SQL on a warehouse via REST

exercises.q: At 9:00, 60 analysts open dashboards; each query is simple but many are QUEUED. What do you change on the SQL warehouse?
exercises.explain: Queueing is a concurrency problem: raise max clusters so the warehouse scales out. A bigger size speeds up individual heavy queries but doesn't add parallel capacity as effectively.
why: Size helps heavy single queries, not queueing.
Correct — scale out for concurrency.
Auto-stop only affects idle time.
All-purpose clusters aren't for BI serving.

exercises.q: Author, monitor/debug, or connect?
exercises.explain: Authoring happens in the SQL editor, queries and dashboards; monitoring/debugging uses query history, query profile and alerts; external access goes through JDBC/ODBC, Power BI/Tableau and the Statement Execution API.

exercises.q: Auto-stop shuts the SQL warehouse down after a period of inactivity to save cost.
exercises.explain: True. Auto-stop stops an idle warehouse after the configured minutes; the next query starts it again (fast for serverless).

exercises.q: Which is NOT a SQL warehouse type?
exercises.explain: SQL warehouses come as Serverless, Pro and Classic. All-purpose is a classic cluster type for notebooks, not a warehouse type.

exercises.q: One gold dashboard query takes 3 minutes; all others are fast and nothing is queued.

steps.prompt: Where do you look first?

options.text: The query profile of that query
options.fb: It shows which operator (scan, join, aggregate) eats the time and how much data is read.

options.text: Raise max clusters
options.fb: Nothing is queued — concurrency isn't the problem.

options.text: Recreate the dashboard
options.fb: The dashboard isn't the slow part; the query is.

steps.prompt: The profile shows a full scan of a huge table with most time in the Scan. Reasonable direction?

options.text: Improve data layout/skipping (clustering on filter columns) or precompute with a materialized view
options.fb: Less data read = faster; MVs precompute heavy aggregations.

options.text: Disable Photon
options.fb: Photon speeds up scans; disabling it slows things down.

options.text: Shorten auto-stop
options.fb: Auto-stop affects idle cost, not query speed.

exercises.q: Order the investigation process for ‘query slow’.
exercises.explain: Go from coarse to fine: Spark UI → the slow stage → the slow tasks inside it → compare their distribution → then test hypotheses (skew, shuffle, spill, I/O, join, GC, small files). Never start with ‘bigger cluster’.
items: Test hypotheses: skew / shuffle / spill / I/O / join / GC / small files

exercises.q: Match the physical-plan operator to its meaning.
exercises.explain: Exchange = shuffle; BroadcastHashJoin = small side copied everywhere; SortMergeJoin = shuffle + sort + merge; HashAggregate = hash-based aggregation; WholeStageCodegen = fused generated code; Scan = reading the source.
pairs: Small side copied to every executor
Both sides shuffled by key, sorted, merged
Several operators fused into one generated function

exercises.q: Match the Spark UI metric to what it tells you.
exercises.explain: Shuffle write/read measure data moved between stages; spill (memory/disk) shows data that didn't fit; GC time shows JVM memory pressure. Uneven shuffle read across tasks is the classic skew signal.
pairs: Bytes written by map tasks for the next stage
In-memory size of data that had to be spilled
Time paused for JVM garbage collection

exercises.q: You need to reduce 2,000 tiny output partitions to 50 before writing, as cheaply as possible. Which call?
exercises.explain: `coalesce(50)` merges existing partitions without a full shuffle — cheap, down-only. `repartition(50)` does a full shuffle (useful to rebalance or increase), which costs more here.

exercises.q: Which bottleneck does each piece of evidence point to?
exercises.explain: Spill, high GC and OOMs mean memory pressure. Long time reading storage, thousands of tiny files or slow shuffle fetch mean I/O-bound. Busy cores with heavy UDFs/expressions and no spill mean CPU-bound.

items.text: Cores at 100%, heavy Python UDF, no spill

exercises.q: When a job slows from 8 to 42 minutes, the first step is to use a bigger cluster.
exercises.explain: False. The plan explicitly rejects blind scaling: open the Spark UI, find the slow stage and tasks, compare distributions and test hypotheses. If it's skew, more nodes won't help at all.

exercises.q: The DRIVER crashes with OutOfMemory right after `big_df.collect()`. Most likely cause?
exercises.explain: `collect()` (and `toPandas()`) pulls all rows into the driver's memory — a classic driver OOM. Executor OOMs come from huge partitions/skew on workers, not from collecting results.
options: A skewed partition on one executor
Collecting a large result to the driver

exercises.q: Match the performance technique to its definition.
exercises.explain: Salting spreads hot keys; broadcasting avoids shuffling the big side; AQE re-optimizes at runtime; compaction fixes small files; data skipping avoids reading irrelevant files.
pairs: Add a random suffix to a hot key to spread it
Send a small table to all executors
Runtime re-optimization: coalesce, switch joins, split skew
Merge many small files into larger ones
Use file stats to avoid reading files

exercises.q: Case from the plan: **Job used to take 8 min. Now takes 42 min.**

steps.prompt: First move?

options.text: Open the Spark UI and find which stage got slow
options.fb: Evidence first: locate the slow stage.

options.text: Double the workers
options.fb: Blind scaling; if it's skew it won't help.

options.text: Rewrite the job in SQL
options.fb: No evidence that the language is the issue.

steps.prompt: Stage 7 (a join) went from 1 to 35 minutes. Inside it?

options.text: Compare task metrics: min/median/max duration, shuffle read, spill per task
options.fb: The distribution tells skew vs uniform slowness.

options.text: Check the driver logs only
options.fb: The driver log rarely shows per-task imbalance.

options.text: Restart the cluster
options.fb: Destroys the UI evidence.

steps.prompt: All tasks are uniformly slower and shuffle read grew 5×; the plan shows SortMergeJoin where it used to be BroadcastHashJoin. Interpretation?

options.text: The dimension table grew past the broadcast threshold, so the join switched to a shuffle join
options.fb: Uniform slowdown + more shuffle + changed join strategy = data growth changed the plan; consider broadcast hints, filtering, or layout.

options.text: Classic data skew
options.fb: Skew shows a few slow tasks, not a uniform slowdown.

options.text: GC is broken
options.fb: No GC evidence was mentioned.

exercises.q: Three are physical-plan operators. Which one is a Spark UI task metric instead?
exercises.explain: Exchange, SortMergeJoin and HashAggregate appear in physical plans. GC time is a per-task metric shown in the Spark UI.

exercises.q: Order the bundle commands for a first deployment to dev.
exercises.explain: Validate the configuration, deploy the resources to the dev target, then run the deployed job by its resource key.

exercises.q: The bundle defines `resources.jobs.orders_job` with `name: orders-job`. Which command is wrong?
exercises.explain: `bundle run` takes the resource KEY (`orders_job`), not the display name (`orders-job`). Validate and deploy are correct.

exercises.q: Write the `targets` section of `databricks.yml` with a `dev` target in development mode and a `prod` target in production mode.
exercises.explain: Targets define deployment environments; `mode: development` gives per-user, prefixed, paused deployments, while `mode: production` marks the real deployment (ideally run as a service principal).

  dev:
    mode: development
  prod:

exercises.q: Match the developer-workflow tool to its definition.
exercises.explain: The CLI drives Databricks from a terminal; Git folders bring repos into the workspace; workspace files hold non-notebook code/config; wheels package libraries; Databricks Connect runs local IDE code on remote compute.
pairs: Git repo cloned into the workspace (formerly Repos)
Run local IDE Spark code on remote Databricks compute

exercises.q: Per the source, Declarative Automation Bundles is the current name for what used to be called Databricks Asset Bundles.
exercises.explain: True (per the source). Bundles describe jobs, pipelines, source files and deployment targets as version-controlled YAML (`databricks.yml`) and are deployed with `databricks bundle …`. Expect both names in docs and tutorials.

exercises.q: Complete the bundle basics.
exercises.explain: The primary bundle file is `databricks.yml` (YAML). `-t` selects the target; `validate` checks configuration before deploying.
exercises.text: The primary bundle file is [[databricks.yml]]. You check it with `databricks bundle [[validate]]`, deploy with `databricks bundle deploy [[-t]] dev`, and run a job with `databricks bundle [[run]] orders_job -t dev`.

exercises.q: Your CI pipeline deploys the bundle to prod. Which identity should it use?
exercises.explain: A service principal: a non-human deployment identity with exactly the needed permissions. Personal credentials in CI are a security and continuity risk.

exercises.q: Interview: why define jobs and pipelines in a bundle instead of clicking them together in the UI?
exercises.explain: Look for version control, review, reproducible multi-environment deploys, CI/CD, rollbacks, service-principal identity.
exercises.model: With a bundle, jobs/pipelines/source files and targets are version-controlled configuration. Changes are reviewed in Git, validated and tested in CI, and deployed the same way to dev/test/prod with per-environment settings. Deployments are reproducible and can be rolled back by redeploying a previous commit, and production runs under a service principal instead of someone's account. Clicking in the UI is manual, unreviewed and hard to reproduce.
rubric: Rollback by redeploying a previous version

exercises.q: You need to run a **scheduled PySpark workload without managing infrastructure**. Which compute?
exercises.explain: Serverless jobs compute: scheduled (a job), PySpark, and Databricks manages the infrastructure. All-purpose is interactive; classic job clusters require you to configure VMs; a SQL warehouse runs SQL, not PySpark jobs.
why: Interactive and you manage it.
Classic = you manage the VM configuration.
Correct.
Warehouses run SQL, not PySpark workloads.

exercises.q: A 2 TB ETL job went from 12 to 45 minutes. One stage has 1,000 tasks: 997 finish in 20 s, 3 run 15 min spilling 80 GB each.

steps.prompt: Most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Data skew — a few partitions hold far more data
options.fb: A long tail of a few huge tasks is the skew signature.

options.text: The cluster is too small
options.fb: 997 tasks finish quickly; capacity is fine.

options.text: Too many small files
options.fb: Small files make many tasks slow-ish, not 3 extreme stragglers.

steps.prompt: How do you prove it in the Spark UI?

options.text: Stage summary metrics: median vs max duration, shuffle read/records and spill concentrated in the 3 tasks
options.fb: Evidence: max ≫ median and the same 3 tasks read far more shuffle data.

options.text: Check the job's total duration only
options.fb: Total duration can't distinguish skew from other causes.

options.text: Look at the notebook code formatting
options.fb: Not evidence.

steps.prompt: Then what?

options.text: Find the hot join/grouping key (e.g. NULL or one giant customer) and apply AQE skew handling, salting, or broadcasting the small side
options.fb: Fix the distribution, not the hardware.

options.text: Add 20 workers
options.fb: The 3 huge partitions still run as 3 single tasks.

options.text: Increase GC time
options.fb: GC time is a symptom metric, not a setting to raise.

exercises.q: In the 2 TB case, 3 straggler tasks each spill 80 GB. How many GB spill in total from those tasks?
exercises.explain: 3 × 80 GB = 240 GB of spill concentrated in 3 tasks out of 1,000 — further evidence that the data is unevenly distributed (skew), not that the whole cluster lacks memory.

exercises.q: Certification-style or engineering-style question?
exercises.explain: Certification-style questions ask you to pick the correct product/feature for a short scenario. Engineering-style questions give symptoms and numbers and expect hypothesis → evidence → fix.

Which command shows a table's version history?

3 of 1,000 tasks take 15 min and spill 80 GB — investigate

exercises.q: Order the verification list the plan gives after hypothesizing skew.
exercises.explain: Start in the Spark UI, look at the task-duration distribution, then shuffle read/write and spill per task, then partition sizes, then identify the join/grouping key, and confirm with the physical plan.

exercises.q: Answer the engineering-style question as in an interview: *3 of 1,000 tasks take 15 min and spill 80 GB each; the rest take 20 s. What is happening and how do you investigate?*
exercises.explain: Look for: skew hypothesis, UI evidence, hot key, fixes, why scaling doesn't help.
exercises.model: It's very likely data skew: a few partitions got far more data than the rest, so three tasks process huge partitions, run out of execution memory and spill. I'd confirm in the Spark UI stage view — median duration ~20 s vs max ~15 min, and those three tasks have much larger shuffle read/records and all the spill. Then I'd find the join or groupBy key feeding that stage and check its value distribution (often NULLs or one giant customer) and confirm the join type in the physical plan. Fixes: enable/tune AQE skew-join handling, salt the hot key, broadcast the small side, or handle the hot key/NULLs separately. Adding nodes wouldn't help, because the big partitions still run as single tasks.
rubric: Evidence: median vs max duration, shuffle read and spill per task in Spark UI
Find the hot key (join/grouping key, NULLs)
Fixes: AQE skew handling, salting, broadcast, separate hot-key handling
Explains why more hardware doesn't fix it

exercises.q: If 997 tasks finish in 20 s and 3 take 15 minutes, the cluster simply needs more workers.
exercises.explain: False. The cluster handles 997 tasks quickly; the problem is 3 oversized partitions. More workers can't split a single task, so the stragglers stay slow — this is skew.
